passage: "Exam dates first," said Hansa, spreading the timetable on the bed. Her older brother Naveen sat cross-legged, holding a pen. "Maths on the fourth, Science on the ninth." "Take away the rest days," Naveen said. "Two before each paper: no new topics, only light review and sleep." "Right." Hansa drew boxes on the calendar backwards from the fourth. "Then I split what remains into revision blocks for each subject, weakest chapters first. So the last new chapter for Maths is here." She tapped a date. "And nothing new after this line." Naveen nodded. "That looks like a plan you can trust." Hansa capped the pen and, for the first time in a week, breathed out.

qa.a: Two days before each paper are kept for light review and sleep.

qa.q: What could Hansa do if a chapter takes longer than planned?

qa.a: As one that can be trusted, since Naveen said so after it was drawn.

subtype: Approach: backward calendar with buffer days [Action]
passage: I'm Parveen, and my Class 12 revision calendar is still pinned inside my cupboard, all crossed out. I started with the exam dates in red: English 1 March, Physics 5 March, Chemistry 11 March, Maths 16 March. Then I blocked two rest days a week in green, because Anjali, my older cousin, said she burnt out doing seven-day weeks. What was left, I filled backward: Maths blocks, then Chemistry, then Physics, English in small gaps. And for each paper, the two days right before it were marked "light review and sleep". No new chapters. That rule felt lazy at first. But the night before Chemistry, while friends were panicking over new topics, I was going over my formula sheet and was asleep by ten.

qa.q: What date was the Physics paper?
How did Parveen feel about the light-review rule at first?
qa.a: Parveen felt it was lazy and was uneasy about skipping new chapters, before seeing how calm it made the night before Chemistry.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do if a block overran?
qa.a: Use part of a green rest day as catch-up rather than cutting into the protected light-review days.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel seeing the calendar?
qa.a: Anjali may feel glad that her burnout story led Parveen to build rest into the plan.

grounding: A student recalls building a backward revision calendar with rest days and keeping the two days before each paper for light review and sleep.

subtype: Approach: backward calendar with buffer days [Action]
passage:
Hostel tutor's note, 12 February — Mridul, Class 10
Mridul brought me his revision calendar to check. He had started from the end: all six exam dates circled, from 2 March to 21 March. Then he crossed out Sundays as rest days. Only after that did he fill in subjects, working backward, with the most blocks for Science and Maths. What I noticed most: the last two days ahead of every paper say only "light review, sleep by 10". When I asked, he said his brother had crammed new chapters the night before a paper and blanked in the exam. I suggested one change, a spare half-day in the middle for anything that slips, and he added it himself, on 10 March. I will check with him at the end of February.
— Gopika

qa.q: Which days did Mridul cross out as rest days?
Why did Mridul protect the two days before each paper?
qa.a: He was worried about blanking in the exam like his brother, who crammed new chapters the night before.

qa.q: What does the spare half-day on 10 March add?
qa.a: A buffer for anything that slips, so one bad day doesn't eat into rest or the light-review days.

qa.q: How does Gopika see the calendar?
qa.a: Gopika is impressed by how it was built, suggests just one change and plans a follow-up check.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a student building a backward calendar with rest days and light-review days before each paper.
